newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Asian spotlight turns on Indonesia's East Timor.
newsitem.headline: Asian spotlight turns on Indonesia's East Timor.

text.p: The spotlight is on Indonesia's troubled East Timor this week with the anniversary of the bloody 1991 confrontation in Dili following an aborted conference on the former Portuguese colony in neighbouring Malaysia.
Residents said all had been quiet in East Timor since a brief disturbance last Thursday in Dili, the capital, over the stabbing of a local man by a trader from another island.
"It's all quiet," one resident said on Sunday.
"There's a lot of military around the city," another resident said, with heavier security evident at night.

But residents said there had been no noticeable increase in tension ahead of Tuesday's anniversary of the 1991 killing of at least 50 demonstrators by troops following a funeral for an anti-Indonesian activist shot dead by soldiers.
Witnesses and human rights groups have estimated around 200 people died.

In past years, the anniversary has provided a focal point for protests against Jakarta's rule and the strong military presence in the territory, which Indonesia invaded in December 1975 and annexed as its 27th province the following July.
"Usually this is a time for disturbances to take place, but probably there won't be disturbances this year," said a diplomat familiar with East Timor.
Diplomatic sources said it took only an insignificant spark or misunderstanding to start trouble. But one source said the strong military presence should prevent any major outbreak.
"There is no doubt that they (the military) are fully in control. If a riot takes place, it's because they allow it to take place," the source said.

President Suharto, who briefly visited Dili last month to inaugurate a series of public works projects, was to be out of Indonesia during the week, leaving on Monday for visits to Jordan and to Italy for a world food summit in Rome.
Indonesian newspapers gave front-page coverage on Sunday to the conference on East Timor in the Malaysian capital Kuala Lumpur that was disrupted on Saturday.
The conference, which had been slammed by the Malaysian government, was stormed by a Malaysian youth group allied to Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's ruling coalition.
There was no immediate official or editorial comment in Indonesia on the incident.

Diplomats suggested other Southeast Asian nations were closing ranks behind Indonesia after Jakarta was severely embarrassed last month when the Nobel Peace Committee awarded the 1996 prize to two East Timorese.

Manila has banned one of the two prize-winners, self-exiled anti-Indonesia activist Jose Ramos-Horta, from entering the Philippines during the forthcoming Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum summit.
"Other countries in the region see possible similar problems at home and are closing ranks," one Asian diplomat commented.

The other 1996 laureate and possibly the most influential person in strongly Catholic East Timor, Bishop Carlos Belo, is reported to have told local people at a mass on October 26 that demonstrations, violence and burnings had to end.
Diplomatic sources said East Timor was one of several factors that had combined to make the local and international business communities edgy over Indonesia's immediate future.

The biggest question mark hangs over President Suharto, 73, who has ruled unopposed for the past 30 years. General elections are due next May and Suharto himself is widely expected to seek a sixth five-year term in 1998 despite his age.
Financial markets have been jumpy since Suharto went for a medical checkup in Germany, and riots sparked by a fracas within a minority political party briefly rocked Jakarta in July.

Local businessmen say despite Indonesia's solid long-term economic prospects, they are nervous about the transition years ahead and speculation over an eventual successor to one of the world's longest-serving heads of state.
